name: Intense pulsed light (IPL photofacial)

card.summary: A broad-spectrum flashlamp treatment used in clinics for sun spots, redness and thread veins, and also sold as home hair-removal devices.
card.note: Hyperpigmentation is the main reported complication, and IPL has been reported to worsen melasma.

quick.overview:
Intense pulsed light is a handheld flashlamp that fires broad-spectrum light into the skin, and the photofacial is its cosmetic skin-rejuvenation use. Clinics offer it for pigmentation, sun damage and visible small vessels, and the same technology is used in some hair-removal systems.

Publicly accessible sources give limited trial detail for the facial uses; the technology is better documented for vascular lesions and hair reduction.
quick.mechanism: A xenon lamp emits light of roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres. Filters remove the most damaging ultraviolet and the longest infrared wavelengths, and the remaining light is absorbed by melanin, haemoglobin and water, heating the targets. Interchangeable filters let one device address different conditions.
quick.risks: Reported complications include temporary side effects and hyperpigmentation. Photosensitising medicines and skin damage are listed as contraindications. IPL has been reported to worsen melasma, and rules for devices and operators vary by jurisdiction.

lead: Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a skin-treatment technology in which a computer-controlled xenon flashlamp emits pulses of broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres, through filters that remove much ultraviolet and long infrared light [1]. Unlike single-wavelength lasers, it can be tuned for different targets using interchangeable filters [1].

People use the cosmetic version, called a photofacial or photorejuvenation, to even out skin tone: the light is absorbed by brown pigment and by blood in small vessels, so sun spots, freckle-like marks, redness and thread veins fade and the face looks clearer and more uniform [1]. IPL was first developed for vascular conditions and is also used for hair removal, rosacea, acne and dry-eye disease linked to meibomian gland dysfunction [1].

Systematic reviews report IPL among the options for solar lentigines, rosacea redness and hair removal [2][3][4]. Melasma is a special case, where light devices have shown benefit but recurrence is high, and a separate reference notes IPL may worsen it [5][6].

chain: Flashlamp pulses are absorbed by melanin and haemoglobin
Pigmented spots and small vessels are heated and break down
Sun spots, redness and thread veins fade
angle.text: A clinic or home IPL device targets pigment and redness in the skin, and users aim for a more even complexion with fewer brown spots and visible vessels. The same technology is used to reduce unwanted hair.

infobox: Vascular lesions 1995, pigmented lesions 1996, hair removal 1997 [1]

paras: Light pulses are absorbed by chromophores, mainly melanin, haemoglobin and water, which heat and are damaged. Pigmented spots absorb melanin-targeted wavelengths, and vessels absorb haemoglobin-targeted wavelengths [1].

Shimon Eckhouse invented IPL in 1992 and filed the detailed patent granted in 1995. ESC Medical commercialised it, and FDA clearances followed for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997 [1].

A 2025 systematic review of 41 trials in 3,234 patients with solar lentigines reported IPL success rates of 74.6 to 90 percent, compared with 27 to 57 percent for pulsed dye laser and 36 to 77 percent for Q-switched laser in the included studies [2]. Photorejuvenation also targets thread veins, photoaging and actinic keratosis [1].
A review of rosacea management says light therapies including IPL and pulsed dye laser are best used for the erythemato-telangiectatic type, in which redness and visible vessels dominate [3].

A 2013 review concluded the literature supports alexandrite, diode, Nd:YAG and IPL devices for long-term hair removal, noted the Nd:YAG is best for pigmented skin, and called for more research on home-use devices [4]. A 2006 comparison cited by Wikipedia found no significant difference in six-month hair reduction between alexandrite laser (68.75 percent), diode laser (71.71 percent) and IPL (66.96 percent) [1].

A trial in 47 patients compared three IPL sessions with nightly benzoyl peroxide gel for inflammatory facial acne [7]. In eye care, a randomized study found IPL plus meibomian gland expression improved dry-eye measures in meibomian gland dysfunction [8], and another randomized study examined IPL for ocular demodicosis [9].

A 2022 systematic review reported that laser and light devices have been beneficial for melasma but recurrence remained high and combination therapies gave the best results [5]. Wikipedia's melasma page notes IPL may worsen it [6].

Hyperpigmentation is the main complication noted. Photosensitising medicines and damaged skin are listed as contraindications, and one manufacturer says its device suits light to medium skin tones [1]. Longer-wavelength Nd:YAG lasers are preferred for pigmented skin in hair removal [4]. Regulation varies by jurisdiction, and a loose split between beauty-grade and medical-grade devices exists, including home hair-removal devices [1].

Human studies include the solar lentigines systematic review [2], randomized trials in meibomian gland dysfunction [8] and ocular demodicosis [9], a clinical trial against benzoyl peroxide in acne [7], and reviews of hair removal [4] and rosacea [3]. A 2006 comparison of hair-removal devices reported side effects of 9.5, 28.9 and 15.3 percent for alexandrite, diode and IPL, all temporary [1].

timeline.event: US patent granted; FDA clearance for vascular lesions. [1]
